request: My partner and I are 31. We want our first home by 2028. Are we too old for ASP, and how much is still left to save for our flat goal?
reply:
You’re well within the age limit for an ASP – it’s open up to age 40, so at 31 you’re fine. For your flat goal you’ve already saved 14 600 €, leaving 15 400 € still to reach the 30 000 € target.

If you keep the current monthly deposit of 425 € into your savings account, you’ll be on track to have about 22 250 € by the target date, still a bit short. You could consider adding the suggested extra 300 € each month (as your payday plan suggests) to close the gap faster.

request: My mum wants to give me 7,500 euros. Is that tax free? She gave me nothing else in the last three years. Please explain whether the threshold itself is taxable.
reply:
If your mum gives you up to 7 500 € in total over a rolling three‑year period, that amount is exempt from gift tax. The tax only kicks in when the combined gifts from the same donor to the same recipient exceed the 7 500 € limit. In that case, the tax is calculated on the whole amount, not just the excess. Since you say she hasn’t given you anything else in the last three years, a single gift of 7 500 € would be tax‑free. For any amount above that, you’d need to report it to the Tax Administration, which will calculate the tax on the total amount.

If you ever get close to the limit again, it’s a good idea to keep a simple record of the dates and amounts, just in case you need to prove the total later.

request: Is my PS balance under 5,000? Can I withdraw it all in 2027? Please explain the exact historical date, conditions and tax. Do not save anything.
reply:
I’m not seeing a PS account balance in your data, so I can’t tell you the exact amount you have saved. For a PS account, the key date is 1 January 2027 – that’s the cut‑off for the 2026 tax year. If the total amount you had in the PS account on that day was €5 000 or less, the contributions you made up to that date are eligible for the tax deduction. After 1 January 2027 the contributions are no longer deductible.

If you do have a PS balance that is below €5 000 on 1 January 2027, you can withdraw it in 2027 or 2028. The withdrawal will be treated as a normal capital gain and will be taxed according to the usual rules for capital income – it’s not a tax‑free lump sum. The exact tax depends on your total capital income for the year and the prevailing tax rate.

Because I don’t have the exact balance, I can’t confirm whether you’re under the €5 000 threshold or how much you could withdraw. If you want to check the exact amount, you could look at your account statement for 1 January 2027 or ask your adviser for a precise figure.

Let me know if you’d like help finding that statement or if there’s anything else I can do for you.
